content: Perineal trauma, which can occur during vaginal childbirth, is associated with both short-term and long-term health complications. Antenatal perineal massage has been suggested as a potential method to reduce the risk of such trauma. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of antenatal digital perineal massage on the occurrence of perineal trauma during childbirth and its associated morbidity. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed, and EMBASE, up to October 2012. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that examined any method of antenatal digital perineal massage performed during the last four weeks of pregnancy. Data from the included studies were independently reviewed and extracted by two authors, who also assessed the quality of the studies. Additional information was sought from the authors of the studies when necessary. Four trials, involving a total of 2,497 women, met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed. All included studies were of high quality. The results demonstrated that antenatal digital perineal massage was associated with a reduction in the overall incidence of perineal trauma requiring suturing. Specifically, the risk ratio (RR) was 0.91 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.86 to 0.96), with a number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB) of 15 (ranging from 10 to 36). Women who practiced perineal massage were also less likely to undergo an episiotomy, with an RR of 0.84 (95% CI 0.74 to 0.95) and an NNTB of 21 (ranging from 12 to 75). These benefits were significant only for women who had not previously given birth vaginally. No significant differences were observed in the rates of firstor second-degree perineal tears or more severe thirdor fourth-degree perineal trauma. However, among women who had previously delivered vaginally, there was a statistically significant reduction in the incidence of perineal pain three months postpartum. In this subgroup, the RR was 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.87), with an NNTB of 13 (ranging from 7 to 60). There were no significant differences between the massage and control groups in terms of instrumental deliveries, sexual satisfaction, or incontinence of urine, feces, or flatus. In conclusion, antenatal digital perineal massage appears to reduce the likelihood of perineal trauma, particularly episiotomies, and decreases the reporting of persistent perineal pain. The practice is generally well accepted by women. Therefore, it is recommended that women be informed about the potential benefits of perineal massage and provided with guidance on how to perform it.
